title: From 1,000 Demos to 8,000 in Three Years — Where Is AI Taking Game Development?

scenes.title: Overview — where the future arrived first
lines: Hello, this is Yamyam Coding.

What you are looking at is the front page of the Steam Next Fest running today. Every blurred tile is a demo whose developer wrote down that generative AI was used. Three years ago this event had a little over a thousand demos. Now it has more than eight thousand.
I think this screen is where the future of AI game development arrived first.

Today we will briefly check what happened at Next Fest, then look at how those numbers changed the people who make games, what players actually got out of it, what happened to the indie market that used to compete on ideas, and what a developer preparing for the next three years should do.
First, what happened.

scenes.title: Phenomenon — making got cheaper, choosing got expensive
lines: Next Fest is the event that gathers demos of unreleased games, three times a year. In 2022 and 2023 it had around a thousand demos; in 2025 about two thousand six hundred, this June about four thousand four hundred, and this October, by Valve's count, more than eight thousand two hundred. Trackers differ a little, but that is close to an eightfold rise in three years.
Across all of Steam, twenty thousand games were released last year alone, and half of them have fewer than ten reviews.

And the day after this fest opened, a Reddit post saying that AI had absolutely ruined Next Fest passed eight thousand eight hundred upvotes. Finding a decent demo, it said, was harder than winning the lottery.
Counted properly, more than 36 percent of this fest's demos disclose generative AI. Four months ago it was around 20 percent.
These numbers say one thing: making got cheaper, and choosing got expensive.
But first we need to be precise about what 36 percent used AI actually means.

scenes.title: Principle — using AI as a tool versus shipping its output
lines: Steam's AI disclosure changed three times in three years. In June 2023 Valve refused to release a game containing AI art, because the rights to the training material were unclear.

In January 2024 it became allowed as long as it was written down. Content made during development, Pre-Generated, and content made while the game runs, Live-Generated, go into the survey, and that text appears at the very bottom of the store page in a box called the AI Generated Content Disclosure.
Then early this year the scope narrowed: only content that ships with the game and that players see and hear. Efficiency gains from development tools are outside the section's focus.
So using an AI assistant while writing code is not disclosed, while making the capsule art or background music with AI is.
I think this line is the line that will divide game development from here on. Using AI as a tool and putting AI's output on screen are two different things.

This year GDC asked two thousand three hundred developers, and 36 percent said they use generative AI in their work. The uses: research and brainstorming 81 percent, code assistance 47 percent, prototyping 35 percent. Mostly tools.

But what is used as a tool leaks onto the screen. A major title released this March shipped with a few 2D props made experimentally during early iteration, and players found them within hours. The developer apologized and promised to audit every asset and replace them.
Among this fest's disclosures, many games wrote placeholder images. A temporary asset that stays to the end: that is the most common accident right now.

scenes.title: Future 1 — the makers
lines: So how is the making side changing? Three things are visible.

First, solo developers and small teams make more. Eight times the demos, twenty thousand releases a year. A reporter who read the disclosures at Next Fest found small teams and solo developers citing limited resources as the reason. Making is no longer the bottleneck.

Second, the makers' feelings are going the other way. In the same GDC survey, 52 percent said generative AI is having a negative effect on the industry: 18 percent two years ago, 30 percent last year, 52 percent this year. Only 7 percent said positive. Visual artists at 64 percent and designers and narrative staff at 63 percent are the most negative. More people use it, fewer people like it.

Third, studios have started drawing lines. The publisher of Manor Lords has written an AI-asset ban into its contracts since January. The reason is precise: it only takes one placeholder from a prototype slipping into a build without being replaced.

The developer of Warframe stated that nothing in its games will ever be AI-generated, and as of this July there is a published list of fifty-nine studios that have declared they do not use generative AI.
So over the next three years the competition moves from whether you can make it to what you can prove a human made.

scenes.title: Future 2 — what players got: quality and price
lines: So what did players get out of this? Eight times the choice, but not better games at a lower price.

Quality first. The Next Fest hub is shuffled at random for the first few days, the disclosure sits at the very bottom of the page, and the first impression is a single small capsule image. One publisher's lead said an AI-made capsule is an immediate turn-off. One games outlet wrote that this fest's worthless vibe-coded slop had leveled up.

So players built their own sieve. The blurred tiles in the opening shot are exactly that. An open-source extension called AI warning for Steam shows the bottom-of-page disclosure as a pop-up and blurs or hides disclosed games in search results. No-AI curators appeared, and itch.io has required AI-generated and No AI tags since late 2024. There is an opposing view: the head of Epic Games called this kind of disclosure a scarlet letter pinned on developers. Either way, the work of choosing has moved from the platform to the player.
Next, price. If making got cheaper, prices should have fallen. They did not. Seventy dollars became the default for big releases, and last year Nintendo shipped an eighty-dollar game.

The average price of Steam's top fifty new releases went from 21.8 dollars in early 2023 to 21.4 dollars in autumn 2025: almost flat over two and a half years. The median fell from 19.5 to 15.6 dollars, but that is because many five-to-fifteen-dollar games sold well, not because the same games got cheaper.

If anything, the cost of making games properly went up. The estimated development budget behind 2025's new Steam releases set a record at 27 billion dollars, and the average indie budget is around a hundred thousand dollars, up 156 percent in ten years.
In short, players are getting more games, in more noise, at the same price. I think this is the picture of the quality loss and the price-to-quality burden of AI use being passed on to players.

scenes.title: Future 3 — the indie market and cloning
lines: And the indie market, which used to compete on ideas, got harder. The reason is cloning.
This August a small studio's Needle In A Haystack Simulator went viral on social media. Similarly titled games started appearing on Steam overnight, and one reporter counted at least fourteen clones.

The clones even copied each other. One team said it found thirteen of its classes inside another team's game with identical names, and an error message copied word for word that points to a shader which does not even exist in that game. The reporter read this as a sign of code decompiled with AI and copied.

The co-op climbing game Peak saw near-identical knockoffs appear on a console store within weeks of going viral, and on Roblox one creator cloned another game within twenty-four hours from a single video and said the AI did everything while they sat and watched.

Korean press covered the same story this week. One Japanese developer received an extortion email claiming its game had been cloned with AI, with no proof attached, and another cut back its development updates to avoid being copied. The developer that cancelled its public demo three days before this fest and switched to a closed lottery test gave exactly this reason: once gameplay spreads, AI-made imitations can ship before the real game.

In numbers, indie revenue was already a narrow door. Of the twenty thousand games released on Steam in 2025, 608, three percent, passed a thousand reviews. Half have fewer than ten. When clones line up at that door first, the time the original has to sell gets shorter.
One market analyst put it this way: good games will get cloned and buried, and players will default to the franchises they know.

Because an idea gets copied the moment you show it, indies have to hide it; if they hide it they cannot promote it; and if they cannot promote it, it does not sell. Over the next three years an idea on its own is no longer a moat.
So two processes appear inside studios: having people re-check every asset before release and record where AI was used, and deciding what to show and when.

scenes.title: Closing — the passed-on cost and a wider sky
lines: To sum up: in three years AI has nearly removed the wall on the making side of games.

In exchange, players get more games at the same price in more noise, and indies pass through a narrower door in a market where ideas must be hidden. The cost the makers saved is being passed on to the players who choose and the small studios who build.
To be a star in a sky that went from a thousand demos to eight thousand, you need three things.
First, use AI as a tool, but let humans own what appears on screen and disclose honestly. Track every placeholder to the end.
Second, spend time where the human hand shows: the capsule, the art, the first ten seconds.
Third, make execution and people your moat, not the idea. Community, update speed and the trust of these people made this game cannot be cloned in a day.
An eightfold wider sky cannot be undone. Players are already building the sieve that picks the stars, and the next three years are the time to make the games that pass through it.
